1.12.2.en: Origen sees that the presence of the four faces together (the lion, the eagle, the ox and the man) is an indication of the return of the holy living creatures to their first tame nature. If in the Messianic age the wolf dwelt with the lamb, the leopard lay down with the kid, and the lion ate straw like the ox (Isa 11:6), then this perfect harmony is realized in the final coming of Christ, where He makes all one in Him, enjoying unity and peace together in Him, where we are found in heaven itself with all the heavenly creation.

1.12.3.en: Finally, we would like to mention what Father Novation, one of the men of the third century, said about this vision. He saw in the fiery chariot a symbol of God's care and providence, He who condescends for the sake of man. In his opinion the chariot is the world and the stars it contains, with their orderly movements. He said that God governs the world by using the angels, who are symbolized by the living creatures. The wheels are the movement of the seasons and the days, and the feet point to the movement of time. The eyes of the wheels are God's providence, from which nothing is hidden. The fire points to the vital power that refreshes the world, or the heat without which the world would stand still. As for the two loins that restrain the living creature, they are the natural law.

1.12.5.en: * I long to see Your heavens!

1.12.6.en: You revealed Your heavenly chariot to Ezekiel Your prophet, and You opened a door in heaven to John Your disciple, and I long to see Your heavens!

1.12.7.en: I want to know: where shall I find rest, O Beloved of my soul?!

1.12.8.en: * In the midst of the bitterness in the land of captivity You revealed Your chariot to Your prophet, so he realized that You are the Maker of history and its Controller!

1.12.9.en: Reveal Your mysteries to me, and I shall be assured that I am carried on Your arms!

1.12.10.en: * Ezekiel saw You in the midst of the wind, the cloud and the fire; let Your Holy Spirit breathe upon my soul, that I may inhale a heavenly breeze; that You may lift me up as on the cloud, so that the serpent may not snatch me; and let Your Holy Spirit set my heart ablaze with the fire of Your love!

1.12.11.en: * Your chariot is exceedingly wonderful, a cherubic chariot, with faces like the face of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle.

1.12.12.en: Count me a chariot and a throne on which You sit enthroned within me!

1.12.14.en: the feelings of my heart as a man of God, the strength of my soul as a lion, so that I do not fear, my gifts and offerings as an ox, a burnt sacrifice to You, my thoughts and meditations, that I may fly like the eagle in the heavenlies!

1.12.15.en: * Grant me, with the cherubim, six wings:

1.12.16.en: Grant me humility and hope as two wings with which I cover my feet, as it were, from sin!

1.12.17.en: Grant me insight and love as two wings, that I may behold the splendor of Your glory!

1.12.18.en: Grant me Your revelations and Your grace as two wings with which I fly to Your embrace!

1.12.19.en: * Grant me, with the living creatures, eyes within and without!

1.12.20.en: Grant me heavenly wisdom, that I may live on earth and in the heavenlies!

1.12.21.en: I see Your heavens, and I long to depart to You!

1.12.22.en: I see the light of Your face, and I am enlightened by You and become light!

1.12.23.en: * Grant me eyes on every side, that I may become all face, and have no back at all, so that in every direction I move I do not give You the back but the face.

1.12.24.en: * How wonderful are these two wheels in Your heavenly chariot, which the Spirit moves without ceasing!

1.12.25.en: How wonderful are the two Testaments, the Old and the New; by Your Holy Spirit I enjoy their mysteries, and I move always toward heaven!

1.12.26.en: Their rims are lifted up from the earth to heaven...

1.12.27.en: That Your word in the two Testaments may lift me up, so that I no longer remain in the dust!

1.12.28.en: * How beautiful You are, O You who sit on the throne, how wonderful is the rainbow around You!

1.12.29.en: Show me Yourself... I want to enjoy You!

1.12.30.en: Grant me steadfast faith in Your precious promises and Your everlasting covenant.

2.0.s.en: 1. Enjoying the experience of the resurrection:

2.0.0.en: 1 And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.

2.0.1.en: When the prophet beheld the fiery chariot, he fell upon his face in complete helplessness, as though he had reached death. Therefore the Lord commanded him: "Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee" [1]. For one cannot speak with someone who has reached death; rather, it is fitting that he first rise, to enjoy listening to the voice of the Lord. If the mission of God's servants is to bring souls dead in sins into the life of resurrection, then it is all the more fitting for the servants themselves to experience the resurrection within them. This is what happened with Saul of Tarsus, who thought that he was able by himself, by his human zeal, his training in the Law, his personal abilities and his gifts, to serve God; but when he met the Lord Christ he fell to the ground as one dead and realized that he was nothing... Then he heard the divine voice: "Rise, and stand upon thy feet: for I have appeared unto thee for this purpose, to make thee a minister and a witness both of these things which thou hast seen, and of those things in the which I will appear unto thee" (Acts 26:16). So he arose and enjoyed the new life of resurrection; therefore he preached to the Gentiles "Jesus, and the resurrection" (Acts 17:18). This is the message of the disciples and the Apostles, that "with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 4:33).

2.0.2.en: Moreover, the command given to the prophet to rise and stand upon his feet carries an indication of the necessity of working without ceasing, for God does not work in the slack but in those who strive continually. For by constant work we bear a divine mark, as the Lord Himself said: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17).

2.0.3.en: The command was given to him to stand upon his feet, fully prepared, to accomplish a holy and weighty mission. He had been deprived of the priestly work because of the captivity, but God calls him to the prophetic work, to present the divine will to a rebellious people. Let him stand in reverent awe before God, listening to His voice with all attention in order to fulfill His will.

2.1.s.en: 2. Working by the Spirit of God:

2.1.0.en: 2 And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me.

2.1.1.en: The command to rise was given, but how can fallen clay rise?! It needs the Spirit of God Himself, the Giver of life, who grants us union with Christ Jesus who rose from the dead, so that we may experience the power of His resurrection in us.

2.1.2.en: The prophet Ezekiel describes his resurrection thus: "And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me" [2]. It is as though he could not hear the divine voice speaking with him, nor enter with Him into the conversation of love, except by the entry of the Holy Spirit into his life. By this he understands the divine words, experiences the divine work, and is able to preach and proclaim by the power of the Spirit!

2.1.3.en: The prophet Ezekiel began his ministry with the opening of heaven before him, to see the awesome divine chariot; he fell trembling, and needed the Spirit of God to raise him so that he might walk on his feet. As for the Lord Christ, He began His ministry with the opening of heaven, so that those present might realize that He is the only beloved Son of the Father, and behold the Holy Spirit of God resting upon Him in the form of a dove. He opens heaven in order to grant His believers sonship to God, so that they may find a place in the Father's bosom, and receive the Spirit of adoption. The prophet Ezekiel was terrified because through the heavenly chariot he receives the prophecy concerning the divine chastisements, whereas the Lord Christ rejoiced because by His baptism He proclaims the forgiveness of sins and the enjoyment of the believers in the New Covenant of the merits of His precious blood.

2.2.0.en: 3 And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day. 4 For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD. 5 And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.

2.2.1.en: If the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of believers in general is to bring them into the resurrection of the Lord Christ, so that in Baptism they receive the new life in the image of their Creator, then the same Spirit works in the servants of the Church, that they may go down to where people lie in the death of sin, and lead them to the joyful proclamation of their resurrection with Christ and their enjoyment of the risen life. This is the work of the servant... It is a work above all human capacity, it is the work of God Himself, and the servant is only a steward of the mysteries of God. This is what the Lord affirmed, saying: "Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day. For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them" [3-4].

2.2.2.en: It is as though God confirms to him the difficulty of the work: the matter requires going down to rebellious people, impudent and stiffhearted from father to grandfather. Who then will lead them to obedience instead of rebellion, to gentleness instead of harshness, and to an open heart instead of its hardness and closedness?! It is the work of God Himself; therefore He affirms more than once, "I do send thee unto them." It is My mission and not yours, that I work in the heart within, create it anew and grant it life!

2.2.3.en: This is what all who labor faithfully in the Lord's vineyard have realized. The Apostle Paul says: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God" (1 Cor 4:1). He realized that he is merely a steward who speaks and works not in his own name but in the name of the one who appointed him. St. John Chrysostom comments on this saying thus: [The steward manages the affairs of his master well without attributing to himself what belongs to his master; on the contrary, he attributes what he has to his lord... Do you want an example of faithful stewards? Hear what Peter says: Why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk? (Acts 3:12). And with Cornelius also he said: "Stand up; I myself also am a man." ... And Paul is no less faithful in his saying: "I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Cor 15:10)... And when the Apostle opposed those unfaithful persons he said: "And what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" (1 Cor 4:7)].

2.2.4.en: The servant, as a steward, works on behalf of his master and not on behalf of himself. Therefore St. John Chrysostom was always wary of the love of vainglory and praise, lest he be usurping the right of God Himself. In this he says: "Surely the mystery of the priesthood will condemn us if we do not use it well," and he also says: [He who enters the work of preaching with such desires (love of praise), what pains and hardships pursue him! It is easier for the sea to be without waves than for such a person to be without troubles or sorrows]. The saint feared for himself as Patriarch of Constantinople, so he said: [I shed tears when I see myself on a throne above the thrones of others, and when more honor is offered to me than to others].

2.2.5.en: It is not the work of Christ's ambassadors to offer eloquent human phrases, nor to display their achievements and glorify their personal efforts, but to proclaim the word of the Lord Himself, and to call to repentance in a spirit of meekness and humility. The word of the Lord is strong and able, for "where the word of a king is, there is power" (Eccl 8:4), and God is the King of kings; His word shall not return void, without fruit (Isa 55:11).

2.3.0.en: The sense of stewardship gives the servant strength, so that he does not fear the work however difficult or seemingly impossible, working leaning on the breast of the One who appointed him, whatever the results may be, as he hears the divine voice: "I do send thee unto them... And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them" [5]. This does not mean that God does not know whether they will hear or disobey, but He speaks thus in order to leave them the freedom of obedience or disobedience, so that they will have no excuse that He judged them with disobedience beforehand. As St. John Chrysostom says: [He did not say this out of ignorance, but lest any of the obstinate say that his prophecy bound them to disobedience].

2.4.0.en: 6 And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns be with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house. 7 And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious.

2.4.1.en: "And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, for they are briers (brambles)

2.4.2.en: and thorns (prickles) with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be afraid of their looks.

2.4.3.en: Be not dismayed, for they are a rebellious house" [6].

2.4.4.en: The divine mission is not easy, for the servant works as though in the midst of brambles and surrounded by thorns that spoil God's tillage, and like one who dwells among scorpions he is exposed to hidden stings. Yet he must not fear people, nor be troubled by their words or their faces, but, as God had previously commanded Joshua the son of Nun thus:

2.4.5.en: "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Josh 1:9).

2.4.6.en: Indeed, God warned the prophet Jeremiah against fear, saying to him: "Arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them. For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land... And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee, saith the LORD, to deliver thee" (Jer 1:17-19). It is as though God threatens His servant that if he is dismayed, not only will He not protect him, but He Himself will terrify him, for He does not work in the heart that does not lean on Him.

2.4.7.en: St. John Chrysostom has presented to us a wonderful example of a father filled with tenderness, so that he loved his people more than the light of his eyes; if one of his children fell into sin, he felt within himself as though he were in great danger, like one in a dark prison, or one sentenced to ten thousand lashes, or confined in a deep pit. Therefore he used to cry out to his children, saying: [I can no longer bear more than this! Stretch out your hands toward me and rescue me]. And yet he was frank and courageous, speaking boldly and with power, without fear, saying: [I am ready to bear everything. Whoever persists in his conduct and does not listen to my warning, I will bar from entering the church as with the sound of a trumpet, even if he is a prince or an emperor. How can I sit on this chair if I do not do what befits it?! It is better for me to step down from it, for there is nothing more bitter than a bishop who is of no benefit to his people].

2.4.8.en: God called the rebellious people brambles, thorns and scorpions, not that the servant should despair of them or despise them, but that he may know the difficulty of the work and prepare for it, and say with righteous Job: "I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls" (Job 30:29), remembering the words of the Apostle: "That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world" (Phil 2:15).

2.4.9.en: Some may object, saying: Why did the Lord call them thus? St. Clement of Alexandria answers: [This is a very great proof of His love, for despite His perfect knowledge of the shameful state to which the people had come, so that He drove them out and uprooted them (from Jerusalem), He urges them to repentance].

2.4.10.en: God speaks with all frankness with His servants, declaring to them the difficulty of their mission, for in every generation they find those who resist the truth; and they must prepare to endure pain and persecution, realizing that God grants them grace to be strong to face the opposing currents, so that the servant may know that the path of service is not strewn with roses, but is the narrow way of the cross, which inevitably ends with the joy of the resurrection. Our God has not deceived us, but He reveals to us plainly the difficulty and distress of the way.

2.5.0.en: God says: "And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious" [7]. It is as though his mission is poured into presenting the word of God as it is; they may hear and repent, or they may refrain from responding to the divine voice... So be it. For the success of the servant lies in his faithfulness in presenting the word of the Lord as it is, that is, being faithful in the divine deposit.

2.6.0.en: 8 But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house.

2.6.1.en: Although God chose him for the prophetic work and knows his heart and his striving, yet He warns him, saying: "Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house" [8]. He feared for him lest, while he preaches obedience to the people, he himself fall with them into rebellion instead of raising them up. It is as though God wanted to affirm to His servant that he should not forget the salvation of his soul and his spiritual life during his service, because many have lost their peace and their salvation during their human zeal and their labor in service. For this reason the Apostle Paul says: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Cor 9:27). This is what moved St. John Chrysostom, whose heart melted with love for the sake of service, to be watchful not only for the salvation of his brethren but also for the salvation of his own soul, saying: [My words are of more benefit to my own life than to those who hear me], and he also says: [I know the seriousness of this office and the difficulty of its work, and the violent storms that sweep over the soul of the priest, for they are more severe in their turbulence than the storms of the sea].

2.7.s.en: 6. Enjoying the experience of the word of God:

2.7.0.en: 8 open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee. 9 And when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein; 10 And he spread it before me; and it was written within and without: and there was written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe. [8-10].

2.7.1.en: The subject of his work is "the word of God," which the servant must eat, so that his inner depths are filled with it, and it becomes the subject of his continual thought, and he even hides in it, so that he presents nothing of himself but presents what belongs to God.

2.7.2.en: Eating the word means its entering into his depths; it turns in his life into blood that flows in his veins. It is as though he is blended with it, and counts it as his life! He eats it and lives by it in order to present it to others by presenting his evangelical life as an epistle read of all men.

2.7.3.en: St. John Chrysostom was accustomed to present to his people from the table of the Holy Bible almost every day, giving special attention to the Gospel and apostolic word. In one of his homilies he says:

2.7.5.en: It is a heavenly trumpet! It is the harp of the Spirit!

2.7.6.en: Yes. The reading of the Holy Scriptures is a garden, indeed, it is a paradise also, which offers not only fragrant flowers but also fruits that can nourish the soul...!

2.7.7.en: We are like men who smelt gold extracted from the apostolic mines, not by throwing it into a furnace, but by depositing it in the minds of your souls, not by kindling an earthly fire but by the inflaming of the Spirit.

2.7.8.en: So let us gather from it small pieces with diligence and effort... for pearls are not valued according to their size but according to the beauty of their nature].

2.7.9.en: He received a book written without and within. Perhaps he meant that the word of God is declared outwardly in letters on paper, but the matter needs the work of the Holy Spirit, who reveals in the heart the writing that is within, that is, the deep inner meaning. Perhaps he also meant that this book contains on the outside the sins of the people and their transgressions, while within it carries God's chastisements for their repentance.

2.8.0.en: As for the writing, as it came in the Septuagint: "lamentations, and a song, and woe" [10]; the following are some comments of the Fathers on this phrase:

2.8.1.en: *The whole book is full of woe for the perishing, a song for the saved, and lamentations for those between the two (that is, those on the path of repentance).

2.8.2.en: Origen * It contains two sorrowful things and one joyful; for whoever weeps much in this time will be saved in the future, because "the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth" (Eccl 7:4), and as the Lord Himself says: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh" (Lk 6:21).

2.8.3.en: St. Ambrose * Written in it are lamentations, a song and woe. The first of these three concerns you if, as a sinner, you repent of your sins; the second concerns the saints who are called to sing, praising God, because praise is not in the mouth of sinners; and the third concerns those who are in despair like you and have given themselves over to uncleanness, fornication, gluttony and base lusts, people who think that death is the end of everything, and that after death there is nothing else, who say: "When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us" (Isa 28:15).

2.8.4.en: The book that the prophet eats is the whole collection of the Holy Scriptures, which makes the penitent lament, the righteous honored, and gives woe to the despairing.

2.8.6.en: I long to work in Your vineyard

2.8.7.en: *You revealed Your heavens to Ezekiel Your prophet, and he longed to serve You; reveal them to me, and I will work earnestly in Your vineyard.

2.8.8.en: Your heavens are joyful and delightful; working with You is a heavy cross, yet it is exceedingly joyful and delightful. How sweet it is to work with You, for You reveal Yourself to those who work for You and with You.

2.8.9.en: *You sent Your prophet to a very stubborn people, but Your Spirit raised him that he might raise many. Grant me the Spirit of resurrection, so that I do not fear death. Death has crept into me and into my brethren, but You are the very Resurrection. You sent him to a stubborn people, and feared lest stubbornness seep into him.

2.8.10.en: Keep me lest in my service I grow weak and fall. Keep me by Your grace and keep Your people.

2.8.11.en: *What shall I offer to my brethren:

2.8.12.en: Here I open my mouth for You to stretch out Your hand with the scroll; I eat it and find it sweet, O sweetness of my soul. This outstretched hand is none other than Your incarnation and becoming man; You gave me Your body, O Word, that I may partake of it.

2.8.14.en: Make it sweet by Your grace, as I acquire Your divine promises.

2.8.15.en: Grant me to accept Your chastisements as a temporary bitterness for the correction of my soul and its edification forever.
